title: ChatGPT for Academic Purposes: Survey Among Undergraduate Healthcare Students in Malaysia
extended_summary:
This paper examines undergraduate healthcare students’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding the use of ChatGPT for academic purposes in Malaysia. The authors motivate the study by noting that generative AI tools are increasingly visible in higher education and healthcare training, but there is limited evidence from Southeast Asia on how students perceive and use these tools, including concerns about accuracy, ethics, plagiarism, and overreliance.

The study used a cross-sectional survey with a validated questionnaire administered online to students at Manipal University College Malaysia. The quantitative component measured knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported practices related to ChatGPT, and the authors also analyzed open-ended responses about perceived limitations using thematic analysis. The study included 443 undergraduate students from MBBS, BDS, and Foundation in Science programs. Analyses included descriptive statistics, univariable tests, and multiple logistic regression to identify factors associated with academic use of ChatGPT.

Results showed generally positive attitudes toward ChatGPT, despite suboptimal knowledge and substantial concerns about reliability and ethics. About 36.6% reported using ChatGPT for academic activities, 65.9% said it reduced time and effort, and 49.0% intended to continue using it academically. Students most commonly used it as partial support for assignments rather than full replacement. Regression findings indicated that MBBS students, Foundation in Science students, final-year students, and those with higher knowledge and more positive attitudes were more likely to use ChatGPT for academic purposes.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT has perceived academic utility among undergraduate healthcare students, but its adoption should be guided carefully because students also reported concerns about fake references, inaccurate information, lack of real-time data, plagiarism risks, and dependency. The authors argue for institutional guidelines, AI literacy efforts, and ethical frameworks to support responsible integration of generative AI tools in healthcare higher education.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on large language models that produces natural-language responses and can assist with writing, question answering, paraphrasing, and related academic tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an academic-use chatbot among Malaysian undergraduate healthcare students, focusing on students' knowledge, attitudes, frequency/purposes of use, and demographic predictors of academic use.

findings.finding_summary: In this cross-sectional survey of undergraduate healthcare students, 65.9% agreed that ChatGPT significantly reduced time and effort for completing academic work/assignments. Additionally, 36.6% reported using ChatGPT to help complete academic activities, and 49.0% said they would continue using it for academic purposes in the future. No causal effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived reduction in time and effort for academic work; self-reported academic use and future intended use

findings.finding_summary: Students reported mixed academic-use patterns and perceptions: 45.8% used ChatGPT to assist with certain sections of assignments while completing most work independently, 41.1% did not use it for assignments, and 9.3% relied on it for most of an assignment and submitted without revisions. Qualitative responses also identified concerns about fake citations, inaccurate information, generic responses without precise prompts, and overdependence, indicating both perceived utility and academic-integrity risks. No learning outcome effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Self-reported assignment-use patterns and thematic analysis of perceived academic limitations/risks

findings.finding_summary: Multiple logistic regression showed significant associations between program/year/knowledge/attitude and academic ChatGPT use. Compared with BDS students, MBBS students were more likely to use ChatGPT for academic purposes (adjusted OR=3.13, 95% CI=1.27-7.70, p=0.013), and FIS students also had higher odds (adjusted OR=1.95, 95% CI=1.12-3.40, p=0.018); Year-5 students were more likely than Year-1 students to use ChatGPT academically (adjusted OR=3.37, 95% CI=1.59-7.16, p=0.002). Higher knowledge (adjusted OR=1.14, 95% CI=1.03-1.27, p=0.014) and attitude (adjusted OR=1.27, 95% CI=1.18-1.37, p<0.001) were also associated with greater academic use.
findings.measure: Academic use of ChatGPT predicted by demographic, knowledge, and attitude variables in multiple logistic regression
findings.effect_size: adjusted OR=3.13; adjusted OR=1.95; adjusted OR=3.37; adjusted OR=1.14; adjusted OR=1.27

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-institution cross-sectional survey with descriptive statistics, thematic analysis, and regression modeling, not an experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of learning effects. The evidence is useful for adoption/perception patterns but remains correlational and self-reported.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived efficiency benefits and significant associations with use, but no causal academic outcome effects or standardized effect sizes. Overall impact is therefore promising but unclear.
